section.heading: 3.3 Trigonometric Substitution
Learning Objectives

list.item: Solve integration problems involving the square root of a sum or difference of two squares.

section.paragraph: In this section, we explore integrals containing expressions of the form $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}},$$ $$\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}},$$ and $$\sqrt{x^{2} - a^{2}},$$ where the values of $$a$$ are positive. We have already encountered and evaluated integrals containing some expressions of this type, but many still remain inaccessible. The technique of trigonometric substitution comes in very handy when evaluating these integrals. This technique uses substitution to rewrite these integrals as trigonometric integrals.
section.heading: Integrals Involving a2−x2a2−x2
section.paragraph: Before developing a general strategy for integrals containing $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}},$$ consider the integral $${\int\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}dx.$$ This integral cannot be evaluated using any of the techniques we have discussed so far. However, if we make the substitution $$x = 3\sin \theta,$$ we have $$dx = 3\cos \theta d\theta.$$ After substituting into the integral, we have

At this point, we can evaluate the integral using the techniques developed for integrating powers and products of trigonometric functions. Before completing this example, let’s take a look at the general theory behind this idea.

To evaluate integrals involving $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}},$$ we make the substitution $$x = a\sin \theta$$ and $$dx = a\cos \theta.$$ To see that this actually makes sense, consider the following argument: The domain of $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}$$ is $$\lbrack-a,a\rbrack.$$ Thus, $$-a \leq x \leq a.$$ Consequently, $$-1 \leq \frac{x}{a} \leq 1.$$ Since the range of $$\sin x$$ over $$\left\lbrack {-(\pi/2),\pi/2} \right\rbrack$$ is $$\lbrack-1,1\rbrack,$$ there is a unique angle $$\theta$$ satisfying $$-(\pi/2) \leq \theta \leq \pi/2$$ so that $$\sin \theta = x/a,$$ or equivalently, so that $$x = a\sin \theta.$$ If we substitute $$x = a\sin \theta$$ into $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}},$$ we get

$$\begin{array}{clccc} \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} & {= \sqrt{a^{2} - {(a\sin \theta)}^{2}}} & & & { \text{Let} x = a\sin \theta \text{where} - \frac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}. \text{Simplify.} } \\ & {= \sqrt{a^{2} - a^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}} & & & { \text{Factor out} a^{2}.} \\ & {= \sqrt{a^{2}(1 - \sin^{2}\theta)}} & & & { \text{Substitute} 1 - \sin^{2}x = \cos^{2}x.} \\ & {= \sqrt{a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}} & & & \text{Take the square root.} \\ & {= \left| {a\cos \theta} \right|} & & & \\ & {= a\cos \theta.} & & & \end{array}$$

Since $$\cos \theta \geq 0$$ on $$- \frac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$$ and $$a > 0,$$ $$\left| {a\cos \theta} \right| = a\cos \theta.$$ We can see, from this discussion, that by making the substitution $$x = a\sin \theta,$$ we are able to convert an integral involving a radical into an integral involving trigonometric functions. After we evaluate the integral, we can convert the solution back to an expression involving $$x.$$ To see how to do this, let’s begin by assuming that $$0 < x < a.$$ In this case, $$0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}.$$ Since $$\sin \theta = \frac{x}{a},$$ we can draw the reference triangle in Figure 3.4 to assist in expressing the values of $$\cos \theta,$$ $$\tan \theta,$$ and the remaining trigonometric functions in terms of $$x.$$ It can be shown that this triangle actually produces the correct values of the trigonometric functions evaluated at $$\theta$$ for all $$\theta$$ satisfying $$- \frac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$ It is useful to observe that the expression $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}$$ actually appears as the length of one side of the triangle. Last, should $$\theta$$ appear by itself, we use $$\theta = \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{x}{a} \right).$$

section.paragraph: The essential part of this discussion is summarized in the following problem-solving strategy.

list.item: It is a good idea to make sure the integral cannot be evaluated easily in another way. For example, although this method can be applied to integrals of the form $${\int{\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}dx}},$$ $${\int{\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}dx}},$$ and $$\int{x\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} dx,}$$ they can each be integrated directly either by formula or by a simple u-substitution.
Make the substitution $$x = a\sin \theta$$ and $$dx = a\cos \theta d\theta.$$ Note: This substitution yields $$\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = a\cos \theta.$$
Evaluate the integral using techniques from the section on trigonometric integrals.

Use the reference triangle from Figure 3.4 to rewrite the result in terms of $$x.$$ You may also need to use some trigonometric identities and the relationship $$\theta = \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{x}{a} \right).$$

section.paragraph: In the next example, we see that we sometimes have a choice of methods.

example.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a2−x2a2−x2 Two Ways

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int^{}x^{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} dx$$ two ways: first by using the substitution $$u = 1 - x^{2}$$ and then by using a trigonometric substitution.

solution.paragraph: Method 1
Let $$u = 1 - x^{2}$$ and hence $$x^{2} = 1 - u.$$ Thus, $$du = -2x dx.$$ In this case, the integral becomes

$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\int^{}x^{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} dx} & {= - \frac{1}{2}\int^{}x^{2}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}(-2x dx)} & & & \text{Make the substitution.} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2}\int^{}(1 - u)\sqrt{u} du} & & & \text{Expand the expression.} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2}{\int{\left( {u^{1/2} - u^{3/2}} \right)du}}} & & & \text{Evaluate the integral.} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - \frac{2}{5}u^{5/2}} \right) + C} & & & { \text{Rewrite in terms of} x.} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{3}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2} + \frac{1}{5}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)^{5/2} + C.} & & & \end{array}$$
Method 2
Let $$x = \sin \theta.$$ In this case, $$dx = \cos \theta d\theta.$$ Using this substitution, we have

$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\int^{}x^{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} dx} & {= \int^{}\sin^{3}\theta\cos^{2}\theta d\theta} & & & \\ & {= \int^{}\left( {1 - \cos^{2}\theta} \right)\cos^{2}\theta\sin \theta d\theta} & & & { \text{Let} u = \cos \theta. \text{Thus,} du = -\sin \theta d\theta.} \\ & {= \int^{}\left( {u^{4} - u^{2}} \right)du} & & & \\ & {= \frac{1}{5}u^{5} - \frac{1}{3}u^{3} + C} & & & { \text{Substitute} \cos \theta = u.} \\ & {= \frac{1}{5}\cos^{5}\theta - \frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}\theta + C} & & & \begin{array}{l} \text{Use a reference triangle to see that} \\ {\cos \theta = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}.} \end{array} \\ & {= \frac{1}{5}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)^{5/2} - \frac{1}{3}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2} + C.} & & & \end{array}$$

section.heading: Integrating Expressions Involving a2+x2a2+x2
section.paragraph: For integrals containing $$\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2},}$$ let’s first consider the domain of this expression. Since $$\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}$$ is defined for all real values of $$x,$$ we restrict our choice to those trigonometric functions that have a range of all real numbers. Thus, our choice is restricted to selecting either $$x = a\tan \theta$$ or $$x = a\cot \theta.$$ Either of these substitutions would actually work, but the standard substitution is $$x = a\tan \theta$$ or, equivalently, $$\tan \theta = x/a.$$ With this substitution, we make the assumption that $$-(\pi/2) < \theta < \pi/2,$$ so that we also have $$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left( {x/a} \right).$$ The procedure for using this substitution is outlined in the following problem-solving strategy.

list.item: Check to see whether the integral can be evaluated easily by using another method. In some cases, it is more convenient to use an alternative method.

Substitute $$x = a\tan \theta$$ and $$dx = a\sec^{2}\theta d\theta.$$ This substitution yields $$\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}} = \sqrt{a^{2} + {(a\tan \theta)}^{2}} = \sqrt{a^{2}(1 + \tan^{2}\theta)} = \sqrt{a^{2}\sec^{2}\theta} = \left| {a\sec \theta} \right| = a\sec \theta.$$ (Since $$- \frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$$ and $$\sec \theta > 0$$ over this interval, $$\left| {a\sec \theta} \right| = a\sec \theta.)$$
Evaluate the integral using techniques from the section on trigonometric integrals.

Use the reference triangle from Figure 3.7 to rewrite the result in terms of $$x.$$ You may also need to use some trigonometric identities and the relationship $$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{x}{a} \right).$$ (Note: The reference triangle is based on the assumption that $$x > 0;$$ however, the trigonometric ratios produced from the reference triangle are the same as the ratios for which $$x \leq 0.)$$

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}$$ and check the solution by differentiating.

solution.paragraph: Begin with the substitution $$x = \tan \theta$$ and $$dx = \sec^{2}\theta d\theta.$$ Since $$\tan \theta = x,$$ draw the reference triangle in the following figure.

image.alt: This figure is a right triangle. It has an angle labeled theta. This angle is opposite the vertical side. The hypotenuse is labeled the square root of (1+x^2), the vertical leg is labeled x, and the horizontal leg is labeled 1. To the left of the triangle is the equation tan(theta) = x/1.

solution.paragraph: Thus,

$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}} & {= {\int{\frac{\sec^{2}\theta}{\sec \theta}d\theta}}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} x = \tan \theta \text{and} dx = \sec^{2}\theta d\theta. \text{This} } \\ { \text{substitution makes} \sqrt{1 + x^{2}} = \sec \theta. \text{Simplify.} } \end{array} \\ & {= \int^{}\sec \theta d\theta} & & & \text{Evaluate the integral.} \\ & {= \ln \left| {\sec \theta + \tan \theta} \right| + C} & & & \begin{array}{l} \text{Use the reference triangle to express the result} \\ { \text{in terms of} x.} \end{array} \\ & {= \ln \left| {\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \right| + C.} & & & \end{array}$$
To check the solution, differentiate:

$$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\ln \left| {\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \right|} \right)} & {= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \cdot \left( {\frac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}} + 1} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \cdot \frac{x + \sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}.} \end{array}$$
Since $$\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x > 0$$ for all values of $$x,$$ we could rewrite $$\ln \left| {\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \right| + C = \ln \left( {\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} + x} \right) + C,$$ if desired.

example.title: Finding the Area of a Region

problem.paragraph: Find the area of the region between the graph of $$x.$$ and the x-axis over the interval $$f(x) = \sqrt{x^{2} - 9}$$

solution.paragraph: First, sketch a rough graph of the region described in the problem, as shown in the following figure.

image.alt: This figure is the graph of the function f(x) = the square root of (x^2-9). It is an increasing curve that starts on the x-axis at 3 and is in the first quadrant. Under the curve above the x-axis is a shaded region bounded to the right at x = 5.

figure.caption: Calculating the area of the shaded region requires evaluating an integral with a trigonometric substitution.

solution.paragraph: We can see that the area is $$\lbrack 3,5\rbrack.$$ To evaluate this definite integral, substitute $$A = {\int_{3}^{5}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 9} dx.}}$$ and $$x = 3\sec \theta$$ We must also change the limits of integration. If $$dx = 3\sec \theta\tan \theta d\theta.$$ then $$x = 3,$$ and hence $$3 = 3\sec \theta$$ If $$\theta = 0.$$ then $$x = 5,$$ After making these substitutions and simplifying, we have
$$\theta = \sec^{-1}\left( \frac{5}{3} \right).$$

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\[\begin{array}{clccc} \text{Area} & {= {\int_{3}^{5}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 9} dx}}} & & & \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\sec^{-1}{({5/3})}}{9\tan^{2}\theta\sec \theta d\theta}}} & & & { \text{Use} \tan^{2}\theta = 1 - \sec^{2}\theta.} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\sec^{-1}{({5/3})}}{9(\sec^{2}\theta - 1)\sec \theta d\theta}}} & & & \text{Expand.} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\sec^{-1}{({5/3})}}{9(\sec^{3}\theta - \sec \theta)d\theta}}} & & & \text{Evaluate the integral.} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{9}{2}\ln \left| {\sec \theta + \tan \theta} \right| + \frac{9}{2}\sec \theta\tan \theta} \right) - 9\ln \left| {\sec \theta + \tan \theta} \right|\left| {}_{\begin{matrix} \\ 0 \end{matrix}}^{\begin{matrix} {\sec^{-1}{({5/3})}} \\$$ Assume that $$\end{matrix}} \right.} & & & \text{Simplify.} & {= \frac{9}{2}\sec \theta\tan \theta - \frac{9}{2}\ln \left| {\sec \theta + \tan \theta} \right|\left| {}_{\begin{matrix} \\ 0 \end{matrix}}^{\begin{matrix} {\sec^{-1}{({5/3})}} \\$$
